articles.title: Stabbed boy felt Huntingdon train attacker 'was not sane'
articles.summary: Anthony Williams stabbed a 14-year-old boy before he attacked people on a train, a jury hears.
articles.body:
A 14-year-old boy stabbed by a man who went on to attack people on a train said he did not feel the knifeman was "mentally sane", a court heard.

The teenager was attacked in Peterborough the day before Anthony Williams is accused of trying to kill 10 people on a train that had to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon in November 2025.

In a video recorded interview played to jurors at Cambridge Crown Court, the boy said: "This random guy… he just pulled out a knife and stabbed me."

Williams, 33, of Langford Road in Peterborough, denies 14 counts of attempted murder - four of which concern attacks prior to the mass train stabbing.

At the time of the attack, the boy, who cannot be named because of his age, was waiting with a friend on a footbridge over the River Nene, before going trick or treating.

Williams drew a knife from his waistband, he said, and "because I was closest to him, he's just stabbed me".

"I didn't feel like he was mentally sane. His eyes were wide open, like he was on something," he said.

"My friend said he was shouting something like 'are you involved?'."

"When he stabbed me, it's like he was there for a knife fight. Like he was waiting for me to pull out something."

The teenager said he had "so much adrenaline" that it felt "like a poke in the chest".

The jury heard the pair ran away and hid in some bushes, where they called the police.

Jurors later watched a video recorded interview with Dawid Taborski, who Williams is also accused of attempting to murder.

Taborski said he was going to a rave with a friend when he heard a man with a "very, very deep voice" asking "are you involved, are you involved?".

He said the man pulled a knife out of a backpack and lunged at him.

Taborski said he told the armed man, "mate, just step back" before he "literally... ran for my life".

Jurors also saw a video interview with William Ogelby, who was on his way to a cashpoint when he was attacked.

A man walking towards him said "wagwan" to him, which he understood to be a greeting, and he said it back.

Ogelby said the man then pulled a kitchen knife out from a rucksack "and he's tried to stab me three times in the stomach and once in the chest".

Ogelby said he jumped back as soon as the man lunged and "in that moment I've just ran off".

"I thought he was going to kill me," Ogelby said.

During the prosecution opening, jurors were told Williams "has some mental health issues which may or may not become relevant during this trial".

The trial has been told that whether Williams carried out the attacks is not in question, but jurors must consider whether he intended to kill those individuals.

Williams is accused of attempting to murder Raza Aslam, Sachin Balakrishnan, Stephen Crean, Kevin Deely, Scott Green, David Presland and Samir Zitouni on the London-bound train between Peterborough and Huntingdon on the Saturday evening, along with Scott Bletcher, Jonathan Gjoshe and Michael Paffett.

As well as the attacks in Peterborough, he is accused of attempting to murder a teenager on a Docklands Light Railway train in London in the early hours of 1 November.

The trial continues, with jurors asked to return to court on Monday.

articles.title: Consumer Reports urges parents to stop using Millie Moon diapers
articles.summary: Consumer Reports is urging parents to stop using Millie Moon diapers after 600-plus reports of infant skin reactions. Here’s what to know and what to do.
articles.body: When it comes to diapers, Millie Moon is a popular choice. The line, which first launched at Target and has since expanded to other retailers, markets itself as a “luxury diaper” made with premium materials and designed to be super soft. But if you use Millie Moon diapers on your baby, you’ll want to pay attention: Consumer Reports has called for Millie Moon to recall its diapers, citing the growing number and severity of incidents reported to the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC). These incidents involve skin irritation and reactions. NBC Selected has not independently verified these incidents. Consumer Reports is advising parents and caregivers to stop using them while the cause of the infant skin reactions is investigated. Read on to learn more about what this news really means — including what parents are reporting, what the company says, and what to do if your baby has been wearing them. Are Millie Moon diapers being recalled? First, Millie Moon diapers have not been recalled. While Consumer Reports has called for a recall, neither the company nor the CPSC has announced one. So, what is going on? More than 600 incidents involving Millie Moon diapers have been submitted to the CPSC this year, according to Consumer Reports’ review of the agency’s public database, SaferProducts.gov. A CPSC spokesperson told them the agency is aware of the many reports and complaints about the product, though it cannot comment on any active or potential investigations. What are parents reporting? Parents have described redness, swelling, blisters, peeling, bleeding and other painful infant skin reactions, some of which required medical care. articles.title: ‘Need a Plan B’: Yemenis in Aden prepare for another war as missiles fall
articles.summary: As Houthi missiles strike Aden, residents stockpile food and prepare escape plans, fearing a return to all-out war.
articles.body:
For Mohammed Abdul Malik, the powerful explosions that have hit Yemen’s southern city of Aden repeatedly over the past month are an ominous warning of darker days ahead.

Yemen’s Houthis have claimed attacks against several locations in Aden, including the international airport, military camps, the city’s port, and the presidential palace – which serves as a base for Yemen’s government.

Fearing that the city could once again descend into widespread violence, Abdul Malik has begun taking precautions. He has stockpiled food and prepared his car for a long journey if he needs to leave.

“I’ll tell you about myself and my close friends: We’ve started buying and stockpiling basic provisions, like sugar and other staples,” Abdul Malik told Al Jazeera.

If the security situation deteriorates further and state institutions collapse, his Plan B is to flee Aden with his family and seek refuge in Shabwa, to the northeast, or Hadramout, to the east.

“We’ve mapped out an exit route from the city. I’ve prepared my car, checked it over, and set aside an emergency supply of fuel. I’m ready to pack up my family and head out at a moment’s notice,” he said.

After four years of relative calm, Yemen’s war has reignited in recent months, particularly since early September, when the Houthis launched a major offensive to seize government-held areas in the west of the country from the Saudi-backed, pro-government National Resistance Forces (NRF).

Within a week, the Iran-backed armed group – also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God – had seized districts in Hodeidah and Taiz provinces, including the port city of Mocha , a stronghold of the NRF, and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait.

A government counteroffensive launched in early October has made limited gains along the Red Sea coast, but at the same time the Houthis have tightened their siege of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, after capturing a vital road linking it to Aden.

Aden had remained relatively peaceful despite the fierce fighting elsewhere, and had become a refuge for thousands of people displaced by the conflict.

The wave of Houthi missile and drone attacks this month has shattered that calm, and has raised fears that the Houthis may be seeking to capture Aden.

Accounts from friends who fled Taiz, where fighting and the siege have driven up prices and disrupted supplies, have deepened his concerns about what could happen to his city.

“Prices in Taiz have already doubled, and the same could easily happen in Aden. If the [Aden] port were to be struck, prices would skyrocket,” he said.

“At work, my colleagues and I talk about what we should buy, what food we ought to store, what our contingency plan is, and where we would go if we had to leave,” he added.

Abdul Malik described how the Houthi attacks have disrupted daily life in Aden, with some families limiting their movements – especially at night.

“When the [first missile] explosion occurred, one of my colleagues went to the school to pick up her son and found the students frightened and gathered together in one place. We go to work and take our children to school, but there is a sense of anxiety and tension,” he told Al Jazeera.

Aden international airport, currently Yemen’s busiest airport, has borne the brunt of the Houthi missile and drone attacks, which have repeatedly disrupted air travel, forcing airlines to cancel or delay flights and divert others to airports elsewhere in Yemen or abroad.

For residents living near the airport, the repeated strikes and explosions have taken a psychological toll on families, prompting some to consider moving to safer areas inside and outside Aden. Ahmed Awadh, a resident of Aden’s Khor Maksar district, near the airport, said the attacks have left children struggling with fear and anxiety.

“An explosion jolts the children awake in terror, leaving them unable to sleep for the rest of the night. Even the sound of an ordinary airplane now strikes fear into my family,” Awadh told Al Jazeera.

He said the attacks have disrupted schools and businesses, prompting families to rush home and some parents to keep their children away from school. Some families have sent vulnerable relatives, including children and elderly people, to neighbouring Lahj and Abyan provinces or other districts of Aden. Others have rented homes further away from the airport.

Awadh, who lives with 10 other family members, said they have taken precautions by keeping children away from windows during attacks. He and his neighbours have also created a WhatsApp group to check on one another after each explosion.

“The [Aden] airport, which serves the civilian population, as well as other civilian infrastructure and residential areas, must not be targeted,” Awadh said.

Aden, Yemen’s second-most important city after the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, suffered extensive destruction in early 2015 during fierce fighting between the Houthis and their opponents, as well as air strikes by the Saudi-led coalition.

Even after the Houthis were driven out, the city continued to experience sporadic clashes between rival anti-Houthi factions, which sometimes turned their weapons on each other.

Adeeb al-Shatri, a professor of journalism at Aden and Hadramout universities, said the latest wave of Houthi missile attacks had compounded the suffering of a city already plagued by lawlessness and insecurity.

He questioned why Yemen’s internationally recognised government had left Aden, its temporary capital and seat of government, vulnerable to Houthi attacks without adequate air defences to intercept missiles and drones.

“Aden is currently the capital, housing both major and minor state institutions. Therefore, the legitimate government must protect it,” al-Shatri told Al Jazeera.

The Yemeni military has claimed to have air defence forces in Aden, with reports of drone interceptions before they reached civilian areas.

Yemen’s Information Minister, Moammar al-Eryani, did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment on criticism that air defence systems have been inadequate in protecting Aden.

Al-Shatri argued that only a small proportion of Aden’s wealthier residents could afford to stockpile food and other essential supplies in preparation for an emergency. Most residents, he said, were already struggling to feed their families.

“In Europe and other stable Arab countries, people stockpile food during crises, but in Aden, people need three times their current salaries just to live a simple life,” he said.

Al-Shatri also challenged the notion that Houthi attacks had brought businesses and education in Aden to a complete standstill.

“People’s movement in the city returned to normal just an hour after the explosion because they have to keep moving to earn money and secure their daily bread,” he said. “If work were to stop, it would lead to a financial crisis, and they would be unable to provide food for themselves.”

articles.title: Trump reverses course, reinstates cancelled campaign rallies
articles.summary: The decision marks a sharp reversal after the US president said he didn’t feel like he had to hold the events.
articles.body:
A day after announcing he would cancel a pair of campaign rallies, United States President Donald Trump has reversed course, opting to put those events back on the calendar.

A source close to the Trump administration told Al Jazeera on Friday that Trump will be headlining, in person, the previously cancelled rallies in Kansas and Iowa ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections.

“Rallies are BACK ON!” the source said. “No one works harder, fights harder, or loves the American people more than President Donald J. Trump!”

Previously, Trump was due to travel to Kansas on Saturday and Iowa on Sunday. But now both rallies will take place on Sunday.

The source said the events were rearranged to include more tele-rallies, which allow Trump to attend virtually.

Republican officials have also not ruled out that an additional campaign event could be added to the president’s schedule before the midterm election.

The decision marks a sharp reversal after Trump told reporters on Thursday, “I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas.”

“We are going to have a strong ⁠Tuesday night,” Trump said of the midterms.

Iowa and Kansas are states that are normally friendly to the president’s Republican Party. Not since 1932, for instance, has Kansas elected a Democrat to a full term in the Senate.

But according to early polling data, voters in both states have trended more towards Democratic Senate candidates this campaign cycle.

In Kansas, for instance, Republican Senator Roger Marshall is in an increasingly competitive race with his Democratic challenger, megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton.

A poll from Emerson College on Friday found Hamilton in the lead, with 49 percent support compared with Marshall’s 45 percent.

Analysts have warned that Republican candidates could feel backlash at the polls over issues like the cost of living, with fuel prices higher than normal due to the US-Israel war on Iran.

Prior to Friday’s reversal, Marshall defended Trump’s decision to cancel his Kansas rally.

“They think that I’m doing so well in the polls that he’s probably got better places to spend his time,” Marshall said Thursday.

Democrats, however, were quick to accuse Trump of abandoning Republican candidates with less than four days remaining until the vote.

David Axelrod, who served as a senior adviser to former President Barack Obama, described the cancellation as a “ strategic retreat ” in a post on social media.

The Republican National Committee argued the virtual appearances would be more efficient, allowing Trump to reach more voters.

Trump is expected to speak at a rally in Daytona Beach, Florida, on Friday to help boost two of the state’s Republican candidates: US Senate nominee Ashley Moody and gubernatorial hopeful Byron Donalds.

articles.title: Who pays for a $1B riot? Europe looks past rioters to their parents and the apps in their pockets
articles.summary: Across Western Europe, governments are reaching past the rioters — to their parents, and to the apps that carry the call to the streets — to pay for the damage caused by sometimes violent demonstrations.
articles.body: PARIS — In France, the bill for a riot could soon be paid from a family’s housing aid. Some people in a violent crowd could be made to pay for windows they never broke. France’s Senate approved the measure 229-105 this week, less than two weeks after cost-of-living protests spiraled into the country’s worst unrest in years, leading to estimated damage of over 1 billion euros ($1.1 billion). In one weekend, police arrested nearly 2,400 people; authorities say thousands of shops were looted or damaged. Fire gutted Limoges’ 19th-century city hall. France is not alone: Across Western Europe, governments are reaching past the rioters — to their parents, and to the apps that carry the call to the streets. And it may not be over. Spanish fact-checker Maldita.es has found calls for Halloween protests in 46 cities in at least nine European countries. Some urge looting. Officials say the aim is to prevent the next riot and pay for the last. Critics warn that widening responsibility could punish people who committed no violence and make others afraid to protest. ‘Rioters pay’ In France, anyone who knowingly joins a group preparing violence could be made to pay up to 10,000 euros ($11,200) for what others destroy. So could anyone who knowingly stays after police order a violent crowd to disperse, for damage done afterward. Collecting is the hard part, a Senate report says: Offenders often have little money, or income the law protects from seizure. The bill would open another source: money the state pays to help families live. French law already generally holds parents liable for damage caused by their children under 18. Under the bill, once a court ruling is final, the money could be deducted from family allowances and housing aid. Senators added the RSA, France’s minimum-income benefit, worth up to about 650 euros ($730) a month for a single person, and even the back-to-school allowance families get for supplies. A minimum amount would remain protected for living expenses. Communist Sen. Fabien Gay cited monthly deductions of 57 euros ($63) from a household receiving RSA. At that rate, repaying 10,000 euros would take nearly 15 years. Supporters say victims deserve compensation and taxpayers shouldn’t carry the cost. One large shop window can cost tens of thousands of euros to replace. After riots in 2023, insurers paid 793 million euros ($888 million) on 16,400 claims, according to France Assureurs, the insurers’ federation. Human rights groups urged lawmakers to reject the bill, warning it could discourage peaceful protest and hurt families who depend on benefits. Seizing those payments “could have disastrous consequences for the poorest,” Nathalie Godard of Amnesty International France said in a statement. The far right backed the bill in the conservative-led Senate. Next comes the National Assembly, where no bloc has a majority. Seizing rioters’ benefits was long an idea of Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally party. Now the government has made it its own, and she leads the polls for next spring’s presidential election. A French word travels the border French students call a protest that shuts their school a “blocus,” or blockade. In Barcelona, it became a hashtag. TikTok posts under the tag called people to Catalonia Square on Saturday, Oct. 24, and QR codes sent them to WhatsApp or Telegram channels, Catalonia’s interior chief, Núria Parlon, told Cadena SER radio. On paper, it was a protest over education. There was no route, Parlon said. No banners. No manifesto. Just groups of 10 to 15 young men looting stores, burning trash containers and smashing bus stops. When police arrived, the looters scattered, said an AP journalist who was at the scene. Police reported 130 arrests, including 76 minors, according to Spanish news agency EFE. Some TikTok accounts promoting the gatherings disappeared, while others advertised new Halloween protests, Maldita.es reported. In one Telegram group, messages urged people to wear masks and gloves and wait to be told of a shop “without police.” ‘You break it, you pay’ In Italy, the argument starts with another family. “Behind that shop window there is a family that has invested a lifetime of sacrifices,” Premier Giorgia Meloni said Oct. 20, announcing a security decree after looting in Milan. Her principle fits in three Italian words: “Chi rompe paga” — you break it, you pay. “And if the one who breaks it is a minor,” she said, “their parents pay.” Parents now face fines of up to 1,000 euros ($1,120), doubled for a repeat offense, unless they prove they couldn’t have stopped their child. They can be made to pay for damage. Holding parents accountable may help, said Claudio Bertolotti, director of START InSight, a security research firm, but “fines alone are unlikely to deter teenagers driven by peer pressure or a desire for group recognition.” Organizing protest violence, even online, now carries four to 12 years in prison. Before the window breaks Telegram and WhatsApp “must shut down such channels when they incite violence,” Parlon said. Telegram spokesperson Remi Vaughn told The Associated Press the company supports peaceful speech and protest, but “calls for violence, vandalism and theft are explicitly forbidden and are removed whenever discovered.” He said Telegram had removed such calls linked to protests in Madrid. TikTok and Meta, which owns WhatsApp, did not respond to requests for comment. Telegram closed a Barcelona group promoting Halloween looting, but a replacement drew more than 2,000 members, Spanish media reported. The French bill would let authorities demand removal of certain illegal calls to violence or looting without prior court approval. If they stay up 24 hours, they could order the web addresses blocked. Those decisions could be challenged in court. The United States is going the other way. Its law generally shields platforms from civil liability for users’ posts, and the Trump administration calls Europe’s rules censorship. Britain shows the limits of takedowns. After three girls were killed in Southport in 2024, false claims spread online and riots followed. A parliamentary committee found that algorithms amplified harmful material, much of it legal. Under France’s bill, money meant to house and raise children could help pay for a looted shop.

articles.title: A woman used her grandmother's inheritance to buy into a Canadian island property in 1981; 45 years later, she and her partner have protected 140 acres of forest while keeping their 20-acre homestead
articles.summary: A woman who used her grandmother’s inheritance to buy a piece of land on Lasqueti Island 45 years ago has helped create a large, connected conservation
articles.body: A woman who used her grandmother’s inheritance to buy a piece of land on Lasqueti Island 45 years ago has helped create a large, connected conservation area in Canada's Salish Sea. Domena Diesing and her partner, Bruce Fleming-Smith, worked with the BC Parks Foundation to permanently protect 140 acres of mature forest on their property. They kept their 20-acre home and surrounding land. The deal was combined with the purchase of the neighbouring 190.6-acre Jenkins Bay property, bringing the total newly protected land to more than 330 acres. By connecting these two properties with the existing Lasqueti Island Ecological Reserve and Mount Trematon Nature Reserve, conservation groups have created a continuous protected area covering more than 1,000 acres. According to an official announcement published by the BC Parks Foundation on 1 October 2026, this connected area is one of the largest protected natural landscapes in the Salish Sea region.Investing an inheritance to save a forestThe story of the land's protection began in 1981, when Diesing moved to Canada's West Coast from Germany in search of a place to settle. She was upset by the large areas of clear-cut forests she saw along the coastline. She decided to use money inherited from her grandmother to buy a share in a 160-acre property on Lasqueti Island. Having grown up around Germany's heavily managed forests, Diesing was drawn to the island's wild and untouched ancient woodland. After meeting Fleming-Smith, the couple built a home among the trees. Over several years, they gradually bought the remaining shares of the property from its other owners. For more than four decades, the couple carefully looked after the land. They tried to limit their impact on the environment and avoided activities such as burning leftover branches and wood from logging. Instead, they focused on keeping the forest and its natural ecosystem intact.Protecting rare coastal ecosystemsAs the years passed, Diesing and Fleming-Smith began looking for legal ways to make sure the land would remain protected after their deaths. The couple joined hands with the BC Parks Foundation and donated part of their property's value through Canada's Ecological Gift program. Under the agreement, 140 acres were placed under permanent public protection, while the couple kept their original 20-acre home property. “We were able to actually make a gesture that would pass on the responsibilities of stewardship that we had felt with our ownership over the years, pass that on to the public and to future generations,” Fleming-Smith said in statements documented by the BC Parks Foundation. The protected land, known as the Jenkins Creek property, is part of the Coastal Douglas-fir maritime ecosystem. This is one of the rarest and most threatened natural areas in British Columbia. According to survey information provided by the BC Parks Foundation, the property contains several rare plant communities. These include Douglas-fir and Arbutus, Douglas-fir and Dull Oregon-grape, as well as Grand fir and Three-leaved foamflower. The area also has several seasonal streams that flow into Jenkins Creek. This creek is an important waterway for salmon and runs through the valley before reaching Jenkins Cove.Honouring a neighbor's fifteen year visionThe protection of Jenkins Creek happened alongside the long-awaited conservation of the neighbouring 190.6-acre Jenkins Bay property. This completed a conservation effort that had been in the works for more than 15 years. The Jenkins Bay property belonged to the late Alfred “Al” Gaensbauer. He was a local warden for the nearby Lasqueti Island Ecological Reserve and spent decades caring for the area's natural environment. Around 2011, Gaensbauer began working with conservationists Sheila Harrington and Gordon Scott, president of the Lasqueti Island Nature Conservancy, to find a permanent way to protect his property. Gaensbauer also took part in local environmental projects. He helped restore local fish populations and carried out the first official nest counts of Pigeon Guillemots living on nearby coastal cliffs. Research carried out on his property by ecologist Terry McIntosh also found rare lichens and mosses, including the Rigid Apple Moss, which is listed as threatened at the federal level. After Gaensbauer died, his family continued working with the BC Parks Foundation and local organisers to carry out his original plans for the land. “Al was very fit and spry well into his late eighties,” Scott recalled in statements published by the BC Parks Foundation. “He built his own home, lifting timbers with ropes and pulleys, and developed an orchard and garden, disturbing as little of the surrounding forest as possible.” Harrington said completing the transfer fulfilled a long-standing promise to Gaensbauer and the local community. It also ensures that the combined 330-acre area will remain protected from development and disturbance indefinitely.A growing network of island reservesThe protection of Jenkins Creek and Jenkins Bay adds to several other conservation projects carried out by environmental groups across Lasqueti Island in recent years. In 2025, the BC Parks Foundation worked with local landowners to protect two separate properties in the southwestern part of the island. Together with the foundation's purchase of Point Young in 2022, these deals created a protected area covering 568 acres around Squitty Bay Park. Andy Day, chief executive officer of the BC Parks Foundation, said the creation of the new connected reserve covering more than 1,000 acres shows what long-term cooperation between local people can achieve. “This great success is another example of what can happen when people care about the land, work together, and take a long-term view,” Day said in the foundation's official release. “Al spent decades looking after this land and wanted to see it protected. Domena and Bruce made a significant donation. Local conservationists stuck with this for more than a decade, and our donor community once again stepped up.” With legal protection now in place, the connected area will help preserve important coastal shorelines, old-growth forests, and fish habitats across the Salish Sea for future generations.You use AI every day. articles.title: Police in Scotland launch Andrew and Epstein royal castle investigation
articles.summary: Media reports say the inquiries are related to claims that women were trafficked to the king’s Balmoral estate.
articles.body:
Police in Scotland have opened an investigation into the time the former Prince Andrew spent with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his associate, Ghislaine Maxwell, at the king’s Balmoral estate.

Police Scotland, which provides law enforcement throughout the country, said on Friday that the inquiries began after it received “information” and that the investigation was at a “very early stage″.

The force provided no further detail about what the information was or what offences officers were investigating.

The investigation was first reported by The Daily Express, which said the inquiries were related to claims that women were trafficked to the king’s private estate in the Scottish Highlands.

“All inquiries are evidence-led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those inquiries,″ Police Scotland said in a statement. “We would never confirm details of ongoing inquiries and it would be inappropriate to comment further.”

Images released by the United States Department of Justice appeared to show Epstein and Maxwell on a shooting trip at Balmoral in 1999. The photos were among millions of pages of documents the department published earlier this year as Congress probed Epstein’s links to politicians, business leaders and other influential people in the US and around the world.

The presence of anyone’s name or image in the files is not proof of wrongdoing.

Several other UK police forces, including London’s Metropolitan Police Service, Thames Valley Police and Surrey Police, are also investigating information released in the Epstein Files .

In February, Thames Valley officers arrested the former prince , now known as Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, on suspicion of misconduct in public office, based on information uncovered in the trove of documents released by US authorities.

The 66-year-old younger brother of King Charles III was held for several hours before being released on police bail pending further investigation.

It was the first time in nearly four centuries that a senior British royal had been arrested.

The former prince has repeatedly denied committing any crimes.

Mountbatten-Windsor’s links to Epstein have caused headaches for Britain’s royal family for almost two decades.

With US authorities preparing to release documents related to their long-running investigation into Epstein, the king late last year moved to shield the monarchy from the scandal by stripping his brother of his princely title.

Mountbatten-Windsor was also ordered to move out of the Royal Lodge , his longtime home in parkland near Windsor Castle. He now lives in a house at Sandringham, the king’s privately owned estate in eastern England.

The former prince’s reputation has been tarnished by his relationship with Epstein ever since 2008, when the wealthy American financier pleaded guilty to soliciting a minor for prostitution. In 2011, the late Virginia Giuffre alleged that she had been trafficked by Epstein and forced to have sex with Mountbatten-Windsor when she was 17.

Mountbatten-Windsor tried to silence the scandal by giving a lengthy interview to the BBC in 2019, but the strategy backfired when he was criticised for offering unbelievable explanations of his behaviour and failing to show empathy for Epstein’s victims.

articles.title: 'No nation left behind' says Burnham after meeting first ministers in Glasgow
articles.summary: The meeting involved representatives from the UK's four nations to discuss devolving more powers to regions and cities.
articles.body:
The prime minister has said the UK's four nations must "move together" to devolve more power to regions and cities, following a meeting with the Scottish and Welsh first ministers in Glasgow.

Andy Burnham said he wanted to ensure no nation was "left behind" after the sit-down, which also included representatives from Northern Ireland.

SNP leader John Swinney said he welcomed recognition that "Westminster is not working for Scotland" and pledged to work "constructively and collaboratively" with Burnham, while Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iowerth said the meeting was "positive".

Both first ministers have called for a wider conversation about independence but Burnham has ruled out referendums.

Scotland 'not like Manchester', Swinney says in dig at PM Burnham

Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution'

First minister says Budget not serious about Wales ahead of meeting with PM

Speaking after the first National Economic Council for the nations in Glasgow, Burnham highlighted plans for devolution at the regional level, saying he wanted to ensure no nation was "left behind".

"It's really important we all move at the same pace together, and I won't allow anything to delay that," the prime minister said.

"Growth can't wait. People need to see improvements in employment and in living standards in all parts of the UK."

Northern Ireland was represented by officials at the meeting amid the political fallout from the Drumcree parade dispute .

Ministers and representatives at the summit discussed handing regions more powers to control employment support and funding for reindustrialisation.

"It's about creating those structures at a regional level and that is matter for Scotland and Wales to decide what that looks like in both countries," Burnham said.

He urged the Scottish and Welsh governments to "work jointly" with the UK government on "a model of deeper devolution".

In the context of reindustrialisation, Burnham added this could be more devolution of innovation funding.

Swinney, ap Iorwerth and Burnham also agreed during the meeting there are too many young people out of work in the nations.

The prime minister said the UK government would look at "arrangements for further devolution of employment support for young people in both Scotland and Wales".

Devolution has been at the heart of Burnham's policy agenda since he took his place in Downing Street this summer.

He claims "rewiring the state" and handing more control to regional mayors and authorities across England will boost economic growth.

The prime minister's devolution at the national level has so far been less clear but Burnham has said he will listen to the administrations' calls for further powers while advocating that they share more responsibilities with local authorities.

John Swinney said while he and Burnham disagree on independence, the meeting was "a welcome start" on further devolution.

"When the people of Scotland take issues into their own hands, the best outcomes will about," Scotland's first minister said.

"To that end, I will work constructively and collaboratively with the prime minister to devolve more powers from Westminster to Scotland - as long as those proposals drive economic growth that is felt in higher wages, better jobs, more opportunities for business to start and expand, and support with the cost of living."

A Downing Street spokesperson said the UK government would review issues raised by the first minister but this would not include a second independence referendum in Scotland.

Rhun ap Iowerth said: "I was pleased to meet with the prime minister in Glasgow today where I once again pressed the need for Wales and the Welsh government to have the necessary tools to better serve our communities.

"I also reiterated the point that further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd and only the Senedd."

He added he welcomed the prime minister's "step forward" on the Welsh government's fiscal and borrowing powers and gave his "full support" in pushing for a stronger relationship with the EU.

The prime minister had "positive discussions" with the Welsh leader, Downing Street said.

A spokesperson added: "The first minister of Wales agreed to start a process to explore how each government could contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode."

articles.title: How Maya Jama went from Bristol native to Celebrity Traitors star
articles.summary: The Love Island host's journey from leaving Bristol as a teenager to reaching the BBC show's grand final.
articles.body:
Maya Jama has gone from Bristol schoolgirl to one of the UK's biggest television stars.

The 32-year-old Love Island host is set to be watched by millions as she faces the last round table in the final of The Celebrity Traitors, due to be aired on BBC One at 08:00 GMT tonight.

But behind the glamorous television appearances and red carpet moments is a story that began in a council house with a young girl determined to make it on the small screen.

Maya was born and raised in Bristol, growing up in St Paul's with a family of Bristol Rovers supporters, putting on song and dance performances for them and charging 20p a time.

Apology after two women's rights campaigners banned

Exhibition highlights memorial to those lost in WW1

Sir Patrick Stewart 'used his stage on behalf of others'

She was born in St Paul's in 1994 and grew up in Bristol with her Swedish mother, Sadie, younger brother Omar and extended family.

Although Bristol is where she spent much of her childhood, she also has strong connections to Sweden through her mum.

She spent time in Sweden as a young child, attended nursery there and regularly returned for family visits during Christmas, Easter and the summer holidays.

Her Swedish roots are something she has spoken about fondly, even recalling getting upset when Sweden lost to Brazil in a World Cup match as a child.

Back in Bristol, Maya grew up around Stokes Croft before moving to the Cotham and Redland area, where she attended Cotham School.

She has previously spoken about growing up in a council house and being surrounded by family and friends.

In a 2019 interview with the Evening Standard, she recalled being a "proper little show child", putting on performances in the front room and charging family members 20p to watch her dance and sing.

Her mum encouraged her ambitions, even when they seemed a long way from the world of television.

Maya's childhood was not without its difficulties. Her mother worked multiple jobs to support the family, and Maya has spoken openly about the financial pressures they faced.

In a 2021 interview with ITV News West Country, she explained how free school meals had been a "massive, massive help" while she was growing up.

She said: "We'd go to the cheaper food shops and my mum would make sure we'd ate everything on our plate because you didn't know when you were going to get your next healthy meal."

Despite the challenges, Maya had ambitions to work in entertainment from a young age.

At 16, she made the move from Bristol to London to pursue a career in the industry. It was a big step, but one she felt she needed to take if she wanted to make her television dreams a reality.

Her first opportunities came through music and online broadcasting. She began presenting a weekly music video countdown for production company JumpOff TV before joining MTV in 2014 as a presenter on The Wrap Up.

She also worked in radio, building her profile through stations including Rinse FM, before landing a presenting role on BBC Radio 1 in 2018.

Her career continued to gather pace, and in 2017 she became the youngest person to host the MOBO Awards, alongside Marvin Humes.

She went on to present a string of television programmes, including Channel 4's Stand Up To Cancer and ITV2's Don't Hate the Playaz, before taking over as host of BBC Three's Glow Up: Britain's Next Make-Up Star in 2021.

But perhaps her biggest presenting role came in 2023 when she became the new host of ITV's Love Island.

Taking over one of the UK's most talked-about reality shows made her a familiar face in households across the country.

She has since fronted further editions of the programme, including Love Island: All Stars.

Now, she is back on our screens in a very different role, competing as a Traitor alongside King Kenny in the BBC's The Celebrity Traitors.

Having made it to the final, Maya is just one step away from victory, a far cry from her early days trying to get her foot in the door of the television industry.

articles.title: Treasury accepts role in staff member's death after inquest
articles.summary: A Surrey coroner raises concerns over HM Treasury procedures following the death of Chloe Moffat.
articles.body:
The Treasury has accepted it contributed to the death of a personal assistant and said "immediate steps" have been taken to tackle outstanding risks.

Chloe Moffat, 26, took her own life in May 2025, the day after managers told her of allegations that she had shared sensitive confidential information, which she denied.

A coroner found a practice within HM Treasury of "informal fact-finding" meetings with employees accused of misconduct had no basis in the ministry's policy and posed a risk of future death.

Responding, the Treasury and the Cabinet Office wrote that they "accept the concerns identified" and "take them extremely seriously".

The Cabinet Office said it would also undertake a wider review of workplace conflict and resolution across Whitehall within a year.

At Moffat's inquest in August, the Treasury was found to have "materially contributed" to her death by not telling her that the likely penalty if allegations against her were proven would be a written warning and not dismissal.

In a response to the coroner's report , the Treasury "accepted the findings in the report in full" and said it had taken immediate action to mitigate the concerns raised.

If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, information and support is available at BBC Action Line

Strengthened "wellbeing safeguards" had been introduced and the use of informal fact-finding meetings had been stopped while a full policy review was conducted, the department said.

Employees facing misconduct allegations would be informed of the possible outcomes before being asked to respond and a suicide prevention framework was being developed, it added.

"HM Treasury has considered these concerns carefully and has taken immediate steps to mitigate the identified risks," according to the department's response.

"While this work introduces some enhancements, much of it is intended to strengthen, clarify and build on the procedures and support already in place."

A Treasury spokesperson added: "The Treasury's deepest sympathies continue to be with Chloe's friends and family, and the department continues to mourn our colleague.

"An independent review found staff acted in good faith and with a duty of care throughout."

articles.title: Tanker with 27 Indian seafarers targeted in first-ever limpet mine attack in Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: A Panama-flagged oil tanker MT LOUISE 1 carrying 27 Indian seafarers was targeted with limpet mines in the Strait of Hormuz, marking the first known
articles.body: A Panama-flagged oil tanker MT LOUISE 1 carrying 27 Indian seafarers was targeted with limpet mines in the Strait of Hormuz, marking the first known successful use of the explosives against a vessel in the area since the US-Iran war began in February.Union minister for ports, shipping and waterways Sarbananda Sonowal said on Friday that all 29 Indian seafarers aboard two tankers targeted in separate attacks on October 29 and 30 were safe, with no injuries reported.In a post on X, Sonowal said, "On October 29, Liberia-flagged VLCC MT ARZANAH, carrying 2 Indian nationals, and on Oct 30, Panama-flagged crude oil tanker MT LOUISE 1, carrying 27 Indian seafarers, were targeted in projectile attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.""All 29 Indian seafarers across both vessels are completely safe with no injuries,"he said."We are continuously monitoring the situations & coordinating with the ship management companies to ensure the ongoing security and wellbeing of our crew," he added.The attacks come amid repeated incidents involving commercial vessels in and around the strategic waterway, a key route for global oil exports, since the US-Iran conflict began in February.The Panama-flagged tanker Louise 1 was reportedly targeted with two limpet mines attached to its hull while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, Reuters reported citing three maritime security sources.The explosives caused a fire in the engine room and temporarily disabled the vessel, maritime sources said. The fire was later extinguished, and the tanker continued towards its next port of call.The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), a British navy agency, said the crew was safe and there was no environmental impact. It did not identify the vessel in its advisory.The incident took place on Thursday, about 25 nautical miles (46 km) northeast of Khasab in Oman, UKMTO said. However, it was not immediately clear who was behind the attack.Maritime security sources told the agency that the incident was the first known successful use of limpet mines against a vessel in the area since the US-Iran war began in February.It followed a separate attempt in September in which the devices reportedly failed to detonate, two of the sources said.Limpet mines are explosive devices that can be attached to a ship's hull. Their use by a small craft raises security concerns in the Strait's congested shipping lanes."The apparent ability of a small craft to approach a transiting tanker, deploy explosive devices and withdraw presents a significant security concern, particularly in the Strait's congested shipping lanes," Greece-based maritime risk management group Marisks said in a note on Friday, Reuters reported.Marisks said limpet mines were first deployed in the region in 2017 and had been used against tankers in the Strait of Hormuz in subsequent years. It said that "limpet mines are cheap and easily available"."The methodology of a small craft attaching these mines on the hulls of vessels in transit is cheap, low tech and very efficient," the group added.Earlier in the day, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said that three oil tankers had caught fire and exploded while attempting to use unauthorised routes through the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media reported.Iran also said it had destroyed an unmanned US vessel in the eastern Strait of Hormuz. However, there was no immediate confirmation from the US military.The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world's most important oil export routes, connecting the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. The waterway has faced repeated security incidents since the conflict between the United States and Iran began in February.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Galway: County Down man among those jailed for planned mosque attack
articles.summary: The three men pleaded guilty to attempting to engage in terrorist activity in November 2025.
articles.body:
A County Down man is among three men who have been jailed for attempting to engage in a terrorist activity, specifically damaging a mosque in Galway.

Garrett Pollock (36) of Kilhorne Greene in Annalong was sentenced to 10 and a half years with the last year suspended.

Darren Gorman (34) of O'Moore Place in Portlaoise was sentenced to eight years with the last year suspended and Karolis Peckauskas (39) of Newfoundwell Road in Drogheda was sentenced to eight years in prison with the last year suspended.

They had made advanced plans to blow up the Maryam Mosque on the Monivea Road between 4 and 5 November 2025 when they were arrested, the Special Criminal Court in Dublin heard.

Pollock also pleaded guilty to possessing an explosive substance which was found in four glass jars hidden in a drawer in his van on 4 November.

On Friday, Ms Justice Caroline Biggs said that modern Ireland is a multicultural and diverse country and that the actions of this group bring shame on the country.

It was, Biggs said, attempted arson with a terrorising message to be spread worldwide.

She added that it was clear that this was intended to be the first of many attacks.

The men were part of the self-styled Irish Defence Army, which Det Insp Alan McDevitt described as a violent right-wing extremist group.

He had previously told the court the group was a splinter of the online Irish Citizens Army which communicated on the messaging app Signal, RTÉ has reported.

McDevitt said gardaí (Irish police) didn't know when the attack was due to take place but the men had plans to use improvised incendiary devices such as pipe bombs and "Molotov cocktails".

Objects seized by Gardaí included cable ties, hatchets, knives, and masks.

Five litres of chemicals were also seized, and were found to be usable in pipe bombs.

They also found sunglasses, balaclavas, can of sealing putty and an Irish flag.

The men had filmed a video on Pollock's phone in Gorman's kitchen in Portlaoise claiming responsibility for the attack.

The footage showed four masked men in tactical gear standing in front of the Irish flag.

In the video, they said they would like "to take responsibility for destruction of first mosque introduced into our great country in Galway".

The court has also received a written letter from Pollock expressing his remorse and shame for his actions.

It heard that Pollock was "radicalised" online after he started misusing alcohol and cocaine.

Pollock, a gym instructor, consumed radicalised content about purported threats that immigrants posed to the community which was described as "emotive, ill-informed and AI-generated".

The court had heard that after making contact with a group and being invited into smaller groups, he found a sense of belonging and became radicalised very quickly and wanted to show them he was committed.

A doctor who assessed Pollock had said his actions were taken in the context of emotional dysfunction, low self-esteem and isolation.

Gorman's defence counsel had previously told the court that his psychological report highlights extremes of submissiveness and vulnerability, that he was a drug user and addict and also had certain mental health issues.

They had added that he had no history of violence, hatred or terrorism.

articles.title: In 1933, New York's High Line carried freight trains above Manhattan; after its conversion into a park visited by six million people a year, the final garden with 2,000 perennials is set to open in November
articles.summary: New York City’s High Line began in 1933 as the West Side Elevated Line, carrying meat, dairy, and produce above Manhattan’s streets.
articles.body: New York City’s High Line began in 1933 as the West Side Elevated Line, carrying meat, dairy, and produce above Manhattan’s streets. Nearly two decades after its first section opened as a public park in 2009, the final garden at West 34th Street is set to open in November, completing a greenway that now welcomes about six million visitors each year. According to People and Time Out New York, the new 34th Street Garden will include 2,561 square feet of planting beds and roughly 2,000 perennials, along with new paving and signage designed to create a proper entrance at the park’s northern end. Read more details about it, as per the reports, below:From freight line to elevated parkThe High Line began as the West Side Elevated Line, with its first train traffic running in 1933. The railway carried meat, dairy, and produce above Manhattan’s streets, serving the industrial businesses and warehouses along the west side. Its elevated design allowed freight to move without competing with street traffic, making it an important part of the city’s supply chain.By the 1960s, trucks had become the preferred way to move goods through New York, reducing the need for rail freight in the area. The southernmost section of the line was eventually demolished, and by the 1980s calls to remove the remaining structure were growing. For years, the abandoned railway sat above the city, largely unused and increasingly threatened with demolition.The turning point came in the early 2000s, when CSX Transportation donated ownership of the structure to the City of New York. Construction on the High Line park began in 2006, and the first public section opened in 2009 between Gansevoort Street and 20th Street. Over the following 17 years, additional sections opened as the park expanded northward along the former tracks.The final garden at 34th streetThe last piece of the High Line sits at West 34th Street and Twelfth Avenue, at the entrance to the Rail Yard Reserve. The area has been closed for construction for about a year, and visitors following smartphone directions often arrived expecting the start of the park only to encounter a construction barrier. The new garden is designed to change that experience with a proper, greener welcome.Richard Hayden, the High Line’s senior director of horticulture, said that when the 34th Street Garden opens, the entire High Line will be open and there will not be a construction shed anywhere on it. He told the New York Times that the design team wanted to provide an entrance experience worthy of the park’s fame and the expectations of its visitors.The garden will be filled with about 2,000 perennials, including sedges, grasses, and Heuchera villosa “Autumn Bride,” a coral bells variety with pale green leaves and white flowers. The planting beds will soften the surrounding urban landscape, which includes a large parking lot on one side and a roadway on the other. New signage and paving will help guide people into the park’s northernmost section.A garden unlike the rest of the high lineOne detail makes the 34th Street Garden especially important. It will contain the High Line’s only plantings rooted directly in the ground. Most of the park’s gardens sit on the elevated structure, where plants grow in soil only about 18 inches deep. At 34th Street, the plants will be able to extend their roots into the earth below, allowing for a more established and expansive garden.Dutch landscape designer Piet Oudolf, who created the High Line’s naturalistic planting style, returned to design the final space. He said the new entrance should invite people in, something he described as essential for that particular place. His work has helped make the High Line a habitat for bees, bats, butterflies, and birds, adding ecological value to a park built on industrial infrastructure, as per TimeOut.The final garden is not the only refreshed green space on the High Line. At West 17th Street, the Prairie Terrace was replanted after spending nine years beneath scaffolding during construction of the neighboring Faena New York hotel. Its walkway reopened last fall, and planting was completed in August, with new vine screens, shrubs, trees, and grasses adapted to changed sunlight and sightlines.Completing a nearly 20 year visionThe opening of the 34th Street Garden will mark the first time the entire High Line is publicly accessible without construction barriers. That may sound like a small detail, but for a park that has expanded gradually over nearly two decades, it represents the completion of an ambitious idea: turning abandoned elevated railway tracks into a continuous public greenway above Manhattan.The High Line’s success has made it one of New York’s most popular attractions and a global model for adaptive reuse. It shows how obsolete infrastructure can be reimagined rather than demolished, creating space for walking, planting, wildlife, and public life in a dense city. The park’s transformation from a working freight line to an elevated garden has changed how people experience the west side of Manhattan.When the final 2,000 perennials are in place this November, the High Line will complete a journey that began with trains carrying food through the city in 1933. The last garden will not simply add greenery to the northern entrance. It will close the final gap in a park that now welcomes millions of people each year and stands as one of New York’s most distinctive outdoor spaces.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Report reveals campaign promoting racist, Islamophobic, anti-Qatar views
articles.summary: Investigation finds that years-long operation sought to portray Qatar as driving force behind mass migration to Europe.
articles.body:
A years-long, paid-for influence operation promoting racist, Islamophobic and anti-Qatar views has been uncovered by two academics, with the evidence suggesting the campaign was intended to serve Israeli interests.

The investigation, which took three years, was published on Thursday. It detailed an operation that likely cost more than $11m and was carried out across 30 countries, including in Europe, the United States and Lebanon.

As part of the campaign, several million internet users were exposed to advertisements on sites like YouTube, TikTok and Facebook that pushed an agenda, according to the report titled Manufacturing the “Great Replacement” .

Marc Owen Jones, a professor at Northwestern University’s Doha campus, and independent researcher Sohan Dsouza, the academics who published the report, called it “perhaps one of the biggest digital influence and disinformation operations ever documented”.

Their report uncovered at least 533 million exposures of social media advertisements promoting anti-Muslim, anti-migrant, racist and anti-Qatar views between October 2023 and October 2026. It added that the advertisements were launched ahead of elections in some of the target countries.

One example, also reported by French newspaper Le Monde , looked at how the campaign had targeted France and found that “a historical analysis of the ads pushed by the campaign’s backers suggests that they repeatedly sought to align with national electoral calendars”, the newspaper said.

“Buying in France ran through the months before the June 2024 European Parliament elections, and UK buying stopped on 17 May 2024, days before the general election was called,” the researchers said.

“Its sustained promotion of anti-Muslim and anti-migrant narratives raises concerns about attempts to shape the political environment ahead of these votes, beyond the formal election campaign period,” they added.

Additionally, the report warned that “the campaign remains active in countries approaching major elections, including France and Italy in 2027”.

France accounted for about a third of the total number of advertisement placements, the highest share among the countries targeted, the report said. Meanwhile, the advertisements recorded the largest number of exposures in the United Kingdom, at 154 million. The US came second, with 100 million.

“In Europe, the ads use the structure of the Great Replacement conspiracy theory, that white people are being replaced by immigrants,” Jones said.

“Qatar takes the role that anti-Semitic versions give to George Soros: a hidden power directing Muslim immigration to ‘Islamise’ Europe,” he noted, referring to the Jewish billionaire philanthropist and frequent target of anti-Semitic conspiracy theories.

Separately, one of the campaigns that appeared on TikTok promoted regime change in Iran to audiences in Europe. The ads first began running on February 24, four days before the US and Israel launched their war on the country, the investigation found.

According to the report, the evidence suggests with “moderate to high confidence” that the influence operation was launched from within Israel and sought to portray Qatar as the driving force behind mass migration meant to allegedly “Islamise” Europe.

The researchers said metadata shows that video editors working on the campaign did so in the Israeli time zone. It also reveals that they used machines with Hebrew drive and folder names.

Qatar has been the focus of Israeli-linked campaigns before. Last month, the Israeli newspaper Haaretz found that a group of Israeli influence experts and political advisers had worked on a secret campaign targeting Doha in the weeks after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attacks.

Israeli politicians have also lashed out at Qatar several times in recent years, with former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett calling for the country to be declared an enemy state.

Most recently, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party accused Doha, without evidence, of interfering in Israeli elections held on Tuesday. The Qatari Foreign Ministry has denounced the allegations as a “disinformation campaign” .

articles.title: How cuts under Colombia’s de la Espriella threaten a key human rights court
articles.summary: Colombia’s president plans to slash spending on a transitional justice court. But war crimes victims fear the cost.
articles.body:
Bogota, Colombia – Angela Cordon was only a teenager when her father and uncle disappeared.

They were among a string of farmers and merchants to go missing in the southwestern department of Huila in Colombia.

First came her uncle Reynaldo Cordon Herrera's kidnapping. A grocer by trade, he had been travelling by truck on January 22, 2003, when he went missing.

The next month, Guillermo Cordon Herrera — Angela's father — set out to discover what happened to his brother, tracing his whereabouts through rural Colombia.

Guillermo called home one night with news: He had made contact with the rebel fighters he believed to be responsible for his brother's abduction.

It was the last time his family would ever hear from him. His body was never found, nor was his brother's.

Angela's father and uncle are among the more than 450,664 people killed as part of Colombia's six-decade-long internal armed conflict.

In the 23 years since their disappearance, Angela and her family have sought any information they could find about their loved ones' last days. "I have dedicated my life to this search," she told Al Jazeera.

She credits one institution in particular with helping her find answers: Colombia's Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP), a transitional justice court.

Set up in 2016 as part of a peace deal between the government and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), the country's largest rebel group at the time, the court handles the prosecution and investigation of crimes committed during the conflict.

But victims, their loved ones and even some former fighters fear that budget cuts could gut JEP, leaving the court unable to fulfil its mission.

This month, the administration of right-wing President Abelardo de la Espriella announced it would enact a 2027 budget with dramatic reductions for government bodies like JEP.

The total cuts to JEP were valued at around 181 billion Colombian pesos, or roughly $57m.

On Wednesday, a Senate committee also advanced a bill to eliminate JEP altogether by March 2028, with a proposal to transfer its functions to the general court system.

Angela, however, credits JEP with offering closure that the criminal justice system was never able to provide. She worries that slashing the court's funding — much less shuttering it entirely — could derail its work.

Through JEP, Angela learned about her father and uncle's time in captivity, as well as the site of their execution. JEP has also worked with former FARC members to try to locate their remains.

"Fewer resources mean fewer missions to the field to find answers, less humanitarian personnel," Angela said, bracing for the cuts.

"It probably means that we will never be able to return to the site."

articles.title: Italy's students take to streets over cost of living, dockworkers block arms trade
articles.summary: Tens of thousands of people, mostly students and workers, took to the streets across Italy on Friday to demand higher wages, better public services and
articles.body: Tens of thousands of people, mostly students and workers, took to the streets across Italy on Friday to demand higher wages, better public services and relief from rising living costs. They also opposed increased military spending and the use of ports for arms shipments amid conflicts in the Middle East and elsewhere.The demonstrations were held in more than 40 cities as grassroots union Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) called a 24-hour general strike. The action was part of a wider international campaign by dockworkers against the transport of weapons through ports and for better working conditions.The protests were largely peaceful, despite clashes earlier this month in which demonstrators fought with police, looted shops and vandalised property. In Turin, however, police used a water cannon to push back students and left-wing activists who approached security cordons around the prefecture building.In Rome, a large march passed near the Colosseum. Protesters said they planned to put up tents and stay there over the weekend. Some rubbish bins were placed across streets and set on fire. In Milan, demonstrators marched onto the city's ring road before ending their march outside the Politecnico di Milano university.In Genoa, around 15,000 port workers, students and other demonstrators entered the port. They protested against the use of ports for arms shipments and highlighted the deaths of seafarers in conflicts stretching from the Gulf to the Black Sea.The Italian demonstrations coincided with strikes and protests in several other countries. Unions in France, Italy, Greece, Spain, Turkey and Morocco had jointly called for an end to wars in the Middle East, including the conflict in Gaza, and “an end to the militarization of ports.”“Ports must not be used for the transport of weapons, ammunition, military equipment and troops,” the joint statement said. “Dockworkers do not work for war!”Organisers said more than 100 ports across several countries had joined the campaign. The action was expected to affect operations across Europe, the Mediterranean and North America.In Greece, dockworkers' unions called a strike at Piraeus, the country's largest port. A separate seafarers' strike over pay, working conditions and safety also kept ships docked at several ports, disrupting ferry services.Giorgos Gogos, president of the Dockworkers Union of Piraeus Port Authority, said: “We don’t want to participate in any war, all around the world. We don’t want our ports to be hubs of military material, transferred so as to kill people.”In Turkey, protesters gathered outside Istanbul's Haydarpasa port under a banner reading: “No to war, no to armament!”In France, the CGT ports and docks federation called a one-day strike at major ports, including Le Havre, Marseille, Dunkirk and Rouen. It opposed what it described as the militarisation of port facilities under European policies and French government budget proposals that it said threatened social protections.The scale of disruption remained unclear, with participation expected to range from full-day strikes to shorter walkouts and demonstrations. In Italy, the general strike caused less disruption to transport than anticipated after the government ordered transport workers back to work.Supply chain management company C.H. Robinson warned clients of possible operational disruptions and shipment delays. However, experts expected the impact on global supply chains to remain limited.Marcus Baker, global head of marine, cargo and logistics at insurance broker and risk adviser Marsh, said a 24-hour strike was unlikely to significantly disrupt global trade, although it could affect perishable goods and time-sensitive shipments.He said the action would further complicate supply chains already under pressure from Middle East tensions, climate-related events including El Niño, restrictions affecting the Rhine and Panama Canal, and shifting tariffs.Judah Levine, head of research at online shipping marketplace Freightos, said the strike could worsen congestion at ports such as Genoa, where vessels already face waits of one to two days for a berth.Ed Anderson, a professor of supply chain and operations management at the University of Texas' McCombs School of Business, said the protests were unlikely to cause outright shortages.“Just one day is not that much in terms of disruption,” he said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Oman rescues 25 from burning oil tanker in Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: Incident comes as Iran says three oil tankers were halted while attempting to use ‘unauthorised routes’ to cross Hormuz.
articles.body:
Oman has rescued 25 crew members from a burning crude oil tanker as ships continue to be targeted in the Strait of Hormuz .

The Omani Maritime Security Centre said in a statement on Friday that it had evacuated the people aboard the RITI merchant ship. Oman said the vessel was flying the Panamanian flag, while the tracking website MarineTraffic identified it as a crude oil tanker.

The incident came as Iran said three oil tankers had been halted while attempting to use “unauthorised routes” to cross the Strait of Hormuz.

It is unclear whether one of the vessels was the tanker whose crew were evacuated by Omani maritime authorities.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said all three vessels were carrying oil and that one was a supertanker. It added that the ships had been halted following “incidents” or after hitting mines.

“Two offending oil tankers, one in the eastern part and the other in the western part of the Strait of Hormuz, which were attempting to pass through the unauthorised route, encountered incidents and were brought to a halt in the waters south of the strait,” the IRGC said in a statement.

Later, in a separate statement, the IRGC said a third tanker – a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of oil – “exploded and caught fire today as a result of attempting to pass through an unauthorised route”.

Meanwhile, to the east of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s navy said it struck and destroyed an unmanned enemy craft on Friday.

Iran has repeatedly warned vessels against passing through the strait without Tehran’s permission.

It has claimed responsibility for attacks on ships and said last month that vessels attempting to pass through the strait without authorisation would face “destruction”.

Tehran has asserted control over much of the waterway since the US and Israel launched the war on February 28.

The US military denies the naval mine claims. On Friday, United States Central Command chief Brad Cooper said the Strait of Hormuz’s “internationally recognised primary transit routes” had been successfully cleared of Iranian sea mines.

articles.title: New York tenants pursuing a mould lawsuit later sought to add a property-damage claim listed at $321,728.79; an appeals court has blocked the amendment over delay, missing records and prejudice to the landlord
articles.summary: A New York appeals court has stopped residential tenants from adding more than $321,000 in claimed damage to their personal belongings to a long-running
articles.body: A New York appeals court has stopped residential tenants from adding more than $321,000 in claimed damage to their personal belongings to a long-running lawsuit over damp and mould. The court pointed to years of unexplained delays, missing receipts and serious unfairness to their former landlord. In a decision issued on 28 October 2026, the Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department, unanimously overturned an earlier ruling that had allowed the tenants to add the large financial claim. The ruling in Dostana Ljusic v Kathleen M. Rodgers Petit rejected an attempt by tenants Dostana Ljusic and her co-plaintiffs to add a claim of $321,728.79 for household items they said were ruined. The original lawsuit was filed in August 2018.Initial claims and missing proofThe legal case began eight years ago when the tenants sued their former landlord, Kathleen M. Rodgers Petit. They claimed that mould exposure at a rental property in Orange County, New York, had caused health problems and made the home unsuitable to live in. According to court records published by the New York State Law Reporting Bureau, the tenants submitted a formal bill of particulars in May 2020. It listed physical injuries they said were caused by mould. However, it did not mention any damaged personal belongings or provide estimates of their value. The issue of damaged possessions first came up in April 2022. During a legal deposition, Ljusic testified that several household items had been thrown away because of mould contamination. After this testimony, the landlord's lawyers formally asked the tenants to provide a detailed list of the discarded items. They also requested shop receipts or other proof of purchase for replacement goods. Instead of providing receipts or invoices, the tenants submitted a one-page summary in October 2022 claiming $70,500 in property damage. Eight months later, in June 2023, they submitted another one-page summary. This time, the claimed amount had increased sharply to $321,728.79. Official records from the Appellate Division show that neither summary included supporting documents, receipts or records showing how the items had been valued.Procedural battles and trial court reversalAfter the plaintiffs filed a note of issue in October 2023, formally confirming that the pre-trial evidence-gathering process was complete, they tried to add the property damage claim through an additional filing. The landlord quickly asked the court to remove the late claim. In April 2024, the Supreme Court of Orange County agreed and granted the landlord's request to strike the property damage claim. The tenants then filed a formal motion in April 2024 under Section 3025(b) of New York's Civil Practice Law and Rules. They asked the court for permission to change their original complaint and include the property damage claim. The landlord's lawyers opposed the request. They argued that adding hundreds of thousands of dollars in property damage years after the evidence-gathering process had ended would put the landlord at an unfair disadvantage. They also argued that the claim was blocked by the legal rule known as laches, which prevents people from making legal claims after unreasonable delays. Despite these objections, Supreme Court Justice David J. Squirrell allowed the tenants to change their complaint in an order dated 25 September 2024. The landlord then immediately appealed the decision to the Second Department.Appellate court finds severe prejudiceIn a decision written for the four-judge appeals panel, Justices Valerie Brathwaite Nelson, Paul Wooten, Laurence L. Love and James P. McCormack ruled that the lower court had made a legal error by allowing the late change. Under New York's civil procedure rules, courts generally allow parties to change their legal complaints freely. However, permission can be denied when the changes cause unfair surprise or harm to the other side. The judges stressed that long delays combined with serious harm to the defence can prevent such changes. "Here, the defendant demonstrated significant prejudice as the plaintiffs' proposed amended complaint was a significant expansion of their claims, was sought after the parties had completed discovery, and was asserted without supporting documentation," the panel wrote in its unanimous decision. The judges also pointed out that the tenants had not given a convincing reason for waiting more than five years after filing their original lawsuit to add the claim. They noted that the tenants had known about the condition of their belongings well before they brought the case. "Moreover, the plaintiffs failed to offer a reasonable excuse for their delay of more than five years in seeking leave to amend the complaint, despite knowing the facts regarding their claim of injury to property for three years prior to the commencement of this action," the decision stated.Strict limits on late lawsuit changesThe appeals court's decision supports long-standing New York legal rules that prevent people from adding large financial claims without proof late in a lawsuit, especially after the formal evidence-gathering stage has ended. By rejecting the tenants' request and awarding legal costs to the landlord, the Second Department removed the entire $321,728.79 property damage claim from the ongoing case. The lawsuit will now return to the Supreme Court in Orange County. The case will continue, but only with the original claims involving personal injuries and breaches of the landlord's duty to provide a safe and suitable home.You use AI every day.
